title: How Candidate Strength Could Define the 2028 Presidential Race
desc: The first 2028 presidential forecast shows Democrats starting ahead, but the real story is how much the nominee changes the race.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: The first 2028 presidential forecast does not just show Democrats ahead. It shows something more important: candidate strength may decide whether 2028 becomes a comfortable Democratic hold, a competitive national race, or a Republican comeback opportunity.

Right now, Democrats begin with a clear advantage in the early model. The average tested matchup gives Democrats roughly a 78% chance of winning the presidency, while Republicans sit around 22%. That does not mean the race is over before it starts. It means the current political environment, combined with the current group of possible nominees, gives Democrats the stronger opening position.

content.alt: The White House or a presidential election scene
content.caption: The early 2028 race starts with Democrats ahead, but the nominee could change the shape of the contest.

content.text: But the important part is that Democrats are not equally strong with every candidate. Josh Shapiro and Gretchen Whitmer currently look like the strongest Democratic names in the model. Both appear capable of turning a favorable national environment into a broad Electoral College advantage. Andy Beshear and Pete Buttigieg also perform strongly, giving Democrats more than one realistic path to a strong general election.

That matters because presidential elections are not only about party labels. They are about how voters respond to the person carrying that label. A nominee who seems broadly acceptable, less polarizing, and connected to key swing-state voters can stretch a party's advantage much further than the national environment alone.

The model also shows a warning for Democrats. Gavin Newsom and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are not irrelevant, but they are weaker in the tested matchups than the party's strongest names. That does not mean either candidate could not win. It means Republicans appear to have an easier time making the race competitive against them.

This is where the Republican side becomes important. Nikki Haley and Marco Rubio currently look like the GOP's strongest tested options. They give Republicans their best chance to turn 2028 into a real contest. Ron DeSantis, Ted Cruz, and JD Vance perform weaker in the current matchup average, especially against Democrats who already have strong appeal in the states that usually decide presidential elections.

The strongest Democratic matchups show how large the gap can become. Shapiro over Cruz, Shapiro over Vance, and Whitmer over Vance all suggest that Democrats could build a commanding position if they nominate a candidate who fits the national mood and forces Republicans to defend difficult territory.

The closest Republican opportunities tell the opposite story. Haley over AOC, Rubio over AOC, and Haley over Newsom are the strongest Republican-tested matchups. That does not mean Republicans are favored overall. It means their path depends heavily on drawing the right opponent and nominating someone who can appeal beyond the party's base.

In other words, 2028 is not simply a question of Democrat versus Republican. It is a question of which Democrat and which Republican. The same national environment can produce very different outcomes depending on whether the race becomes Shapiro versus Cruz, Whitmer versus Vance, Haley versus AOC, or Rubio versus Newsom.

content.caption: Swing states like Pennsylvania could decide whether the Democratic edge becomes durable or fragile.

content.text: Pennsylvania is a good example of why candidate strength matters. A Democrat like Shapiro starts with obvious home-state advantages, but the broader point is not just about Pennsylvania. It is about the type of candidate who can compete in the states that decide the Electoral College. The model rewards candidates who appear stronger in those places, not just candidates who are popular with national political audiences.

This is still an early forecast. Polling is limited, the campaign has not truly begun, and the final nominee list could look different from the names being tested now. But early does not mean meaningless. Early models can show the shape of the race before the campaign noise takes over.

The takeaway should be clear. Democrats start 2028 ahead, but their advantage is not automatic. Republicans start behind, but they are not locked out. The race may come down to whether each party chooses a nominee who expands their map or one who gives the other side an opening.
For now, the first 2028 forecast points to a Democratic edge. But more than anything, it points to a simple political reality: parties do not just need a nominee. They need the right nominee.

title: What Our Backtest Says About the Senate Model
dek: Our Senate model is still being tested, but the early signs are good. The archived-input backtest is the main score, while the current diagnostic is mostly a tool for spotting possible weak points.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: Our Senate model is still being tested, but the early results are looking good.
When people look at a forecast, they might first wonder if it picked the winner. That matters, but a good forecast also needs reasonable odds.
For example, if a model says a candidate has a 65% chance to win, then candidates with similar odds should win around 65% of the time. This is what calibration means.
When we published the current calibration findings, the page had two different sections that I poorly formatted unintentionally, and they are easy to mix up.

The more important section is the archived-input historical backtest. This means we use the model and put in information about a race that it might have had before Election Day. Then we test it against the result in historical elections, such as 2024, 2018, 2016, and other cycles.
Basically, if the model existed before this election, how accurate would it have been? This is key in seeing if the model can be called strong as we move closer to Election Day.
That archived-input test is the main test readers should focus on.
Currently, the archived-input test only has 11 races from the 2024 Senate elections. This is a small sample, so it is not the final word, but it gives an early check.

So far, the model is doing well. In the 50-60% range, the model got all races correct. In the 60-70% range, it got 3 out of the 4 races correct. In the 70-80% range, it got all races correct. In the 80-90% range, it got all races correct.
This does not mean we have the perfect model. A few races are not enough to prove that. It does, however, show that the model is placing races into fair probability ranges.

The other section is the current diagnostic. This means it is a rough check for problems. It compares the current version of the model to older Senate results. This helps find weak spots, but it is not clean or the proper way to judge the model.

The current diagnostic has 35 races, which might sound better because of the larger sample size. However, the comparisons are less direct. States are compared from 2016 or 2018. Some had very different candidates, little polling, independents, or special state-level factors.
The current diagnostic is a warning system, not a grade. The archived-input test, in comparison, is properly organized to be a fair assessment.

Even with this issue, the current diagnostic seems mixed but not negative. The 60-70% range has a 62.5% win rate, which is close to the expected 65%. The 90-100% range had a 95% win rate, which was spot on.
However, the weakest part is the 80-90% range, which had only a 33.3% win rate. Though admittedly, this came from just three races, which is hardly enough to be proof of a big issue.

The archived-input margin misses appear normal. The largest was Pennsylvania at 5.2 points, Wisconsin at 4.2, Ohio at 3.6, Nebraska at 3.4, Nevada at 3.3, Florida at 2.8, and so on, going closer and closer to the actual margin.

For Senate races, this is not alarming. Senate races are hard to forecast because of late movements and state-by-state differences in factors. If a model misses a couple races by 2-5 points, that is within range, though not preferable.
We will get a clearer picture once the archived-input backtesting is complete.
A Brier score is also included in the public release. A Brier score measures how close the model's probabilities were to the final results. We are looking for a lower score as the better outcome.
The current diagnostic has a mean score of 0.134. This is useful, but should be read with caution like the rest of the diagnostic.

The page has a mean margin miss of 12.5 points with the current diagnostic. Due to the nature of the rougher diagnostic test, this is expected, and the cleaner archived-input backtest will show the final average miss.
Some of those comparisons are not a fair one-to-one test of what the model would have forecast before a real election.
This is the main issue with our calibration page. We have two different systems of calibrating that should be interpreted totally differently.
By May 23rd, 2026, we plan to finish the calibration and the cleanup thereafter to properly convey the accuracy of the model with complete transparency.

After this, readers will have clearer answers to some accuracy questions. How did the model perform when tested against past elections and their inputs? Which numbers are only meant to catch possible problems? Which results should be used to judge the model?

Honestly, the model is not fully proven yet. We await the archived-input test to be finished and have it be proven or disproven. The current diagnostic does include some noisy comparisons, which dull any ability it has to prove much.
What we have now, however, does not show a bad model. The archived-input test looks promising. The largest misses are fair, and several probability ranges are lining up as they should.
The model is still being improved, but the early signs are good. To summarize, the archived-input backtest is the main score, and the diagnostic is a tool for spotting possible weak points.
Once we finish by May 23rd, judging it should be easier and more final.

title: How Dan Osborn has Redefined the Democratic Strategy of the Deep Red
dek: Dan Osborn's Senate campaigns show a different path for Democrats in deep-red states. In places where the party label struggles, an independent with local credibility may perform better than a standard Democratic nominee.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: Dan Osborn has changed how you should think about deep-red Senate races.

Nebraska is not considered in any pathway to victory for Democrats in 2026 when it comes to the Senate. This is in large part because Republicans dominate the state. Democrats struggle in deep-red Nebraska due to negative brand recognition. AP reported that Nebraska Democrats in 2026 are looking for others who can "outperform the Democratic label."

Osborn is in a different form. He ran as an independent in 2024 and is running again in 2026. He leans on his background as a mechanic, Navy veteran, National Guardsman, and union leader. He campaigns on workers' rights, wages, corporate power, and taking money out of politics.

We saw what happened in 2024. Osborn lost to Republican Senator Deb Fischer, but the race was shockingly close historically in Nebraska. Fischer won by only about six points, while in 2024, the state voted for Donald Trump by over 20 points. What we learned was simple. Some voters who might reject national Democrats would still consider a candidate who sounds local, independent, and focused on economics.

Just last week, Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary in Nebraska. She campaigned simply on withdrawing and supporting Osborn. This reduces a split anti-Ricketts vote and avoids a three-way race, which all but guarantees Republicans hold on in the state.

Nebraska Democrats appeared to understand that when Nebraska's race focuses on the national aspect, Ricketts wins. When it goes local, Osborn stands to benefit. This is what Democrats need to study. Sometimes in a deep-red state, stepping aside is more strategic.

Of course, this does not work anywhere. You need someone with local credibility and a message voters believe. In a state where voters have histories of ticket splitting or independents, it might be the right move. However, national Democrats must stay disciplined. If these independents are turned into Republican versus not Republican, the brand is weakened.

Even if what the forecast model says holds, and Osborn loses, the current projected margin of only 3.9 points Republican shares a big message. Democrats must reinvent their strategies in the deep red, or become a figment of the past for those living in red states.
The takeaway should be clear. In deep-red states, Democrats need more flexibility. Sometimes the best Democratic move is to support a candidate who does not run as a Democrat.
